title: Review: talking about your people
why: This review brings together the whole unit: possessives and family words, physical and character description, tastes with aimer and the definite article, and object pronouns. Looking at family photos with a friend in Nantes, you put it all to work in one natural conversation.

My people: possessives and description

This unit gave you everything you need to talk about the people in your life. Let's review it piece by piece, starting with the possessives and the way you describe someone.

masc.fem.plural
mymonmames
your (tu)tontates
his / hersonsases
ournotrenotrenos
your (vous)votrevotrevos
theirleurleurleurs
  • The possessive agrees with the thing owned: Pierre et sa femme, Julie et son mari.
  • Mon / ton / son before a feminine noun starting with a vowel: mon amie, son école.
  • No “'s”: la sœur de Paul, then sa sœur.

Describing someone

Three verbs do almost all the work: être + adjective (Elle est grande et rousse), avoir + les for eyes and hair (Il a les yeux marron et les cheveux courts), and porter (Elle porte des lunettes). Adjectives agree with the person:

MasculineFemininePattern
blondblonde+ e
curieuxcurieuse-eux → -euse
sportifsportive-if → -ive
travailleurtravailleuse-eur → -euse
discretdiscrète-et → -ète
gentilgentille-il → -ille
rouxrousseirregular
Mon beau-frère est grand et brun. Il ressemble à son père : il est très calme et un peu timide.My brother-in-law is tall and dark-haired. He looks like his father: he's very calm and a bit shy.
", "

Tastes and pronouns

To say what people like, remember the definite article after aimer, adorer, détester and préférer, even in the negative: Ma nièce adore le chocolat, Mon père n'aime pas la musique classique. After these verbs, a second verb stays in the infinitive: Mes parents aiment voyager.

They say…AgreeDisagree
J'adore les chats.Moi aussi.Pas moi.
Je n'aime pas les chats.Moi non plus.Moi si.

And for hobbies: jouer au foot (sports, games), jouer du piano (instruments), faire de la natation (activities).

Le, la, les: don't repeat, replace

Object pronouns are perfect for talking about people and their tastes without repeating names. They go before the verb, or before the infinitive when there is one:

Le chocolat ? Ma nièce l'adore.Chocolate? My niece loves it.
Mes cousins ? Je ne les connais pas bien.My cousins? I don't know them well.
Ta grand-mère ? Je veux la rencontrer !Your grandmother? I want to meet her!
Les photos de famille ? Je les regarde avec ma mère.The family photos? I look at them with my mother.

A pronoun replaces a noun with le / la / les or a possessive in front of it: mon frère → le, ses amies → les. With aimer and a person, je l'aime means love; for a friend, say je l'aime bien.

", "

Putting it together: talking about a photo

Looking at family photos is a classic moment in France, and it uses everything in this unit. Here are the phrases you need to show who is where.

FrenchEnglish
C'est qui, sur la photo ? / Qui est-ce ?Who's that in the picture?
Sur la photo, il y a…In the picture, there is / are…
À gauche, c'est ma tante.On the left, that's my aunt.
Au milieu, ce sont mes grands-parents.In the middle, those are my grandparents.
Devant, c'est mon neveu, et derrière, ma belle-sœur.In front, that's my nephew, and behind, my sister-in-law.
C'est au mariage de mon frère.It's at my brother's wedding.

Notice: a photo is something you're “on” in French, not “in”: sur la photo.

Common mistakes to avoid

Not thisBut this
Léa et sa frèreLéa et son frère
ma amiemon amie
j'aime chocolatj'aime le chocolat
je n'aime pas de caféje n'aime pas le café
je connais laje la connais
— Je n'aime pas ça. — Moi aussi.— Je n'aime pas ça. — Moi non plus.

When you show someone your photos, French people often react with Il est mignon ! / Elle est mignonne ! (He's / She's cute!) for children, or Vous vous ressemblez ! (You look alike!).
